corrections.before: On 25 July 2005, a Piper Aircraft Corporation's aircraft overran runway 27 at Nhill aerodrome following a rejected night takeoff. The aircraft was being operated on an instrument flight rules charter flight to Charlton, with the pilot and three passengers on board. The pilot reported that, during the pre-flight preparation he set the elevator trim to the take-off position by winding the trim wheel. The pilot recalled removing the lock from the control column prior to starting the engines for departure. The operator's Operations Manual included a series of checklists to be used during operation of the aircraft. The 'Start Up' and 'Pre takeoff' checklists included checking full and free movement of the flight controls. The pilot stated that the take-off roll was from a rolling start with power being slowly applied until engine output stabilized. At about 90 kts indicated air speed, the pilot attempted to rotate the aircraft but encountered resistance to rearward movement of the control column. He decided to reject the takeoff because the aircraft speed at the time was below his nominated decision speed of 100 kts. The pilot then reduced the engine power to idle and applied maximum braking. After the aircraft came to a stop160 m beyond the end of the runway, the pilot exited the aircraft via the crew door, assisted the passengers to evacuate the aircraft through the rear cabin door and marshalled them to an area away from the aircraft. A passenger then used a mobile phone to contact emergency services, who attended the scene soon after.

corrections.before: A runway incursion occurred at Sydeny airport on Tuesday. CSN321, bound for London, was holding short of runway. Meanwhile, JAL578 was on long final for landing. After receiving reports from both flight, the tower controller asked CSN321 to line up and wait after the JAL578 landing. At that time, the radio communication broke down. The rear part of instruction was interrupted by static noise. The pilot of CSN321 misunderstood that he was cleared for departure, and then lined up. The tower controller identified the potential danger. Without hesitation, he instructed JAL578 to pull up immediately and initiate go-around in an attempt to avoid collision. corrections.before: On October 4th, 2010, International Flight 142 was cleared by ATC to follow the VOR/DME approach to runway 36L. But the captain decided to request for RNAV approach regardless of the fact that his aircraft was not equipped with mandatory navigation equipment (GNSS)required for RNAV approach. The Approach controller found the flight being right of track and asked cockpit crew to verify it. The Captain quickly asked first officer to tell the Approach that they were following RNAV procedure. Actually, the cockpit crew was carrying out VOR/DME approach. The captain kept flying the aircraft with no visual cues due to poor visibility. Increased stress level, loss of situational awareness and reduced mental ability caused the pilots flying low on approach with high speed. The aircraft bounced on the runway after touchdown and skidded off. All passengers were safely evacuated, but the aircraft wings and two engines sustained extensive damage after landing gears collapsed.

corrections.before:
A man was on a flight from Seattle to San Francisco, but along the way, the plane stopped unexpectedly in Sacramento. The flight attendant explained the situation and told passengers that they could get off the aircraft for a walk within 50 minutes before the plane re-boarded.
Passengers got off the plane in succession except one person. When the man walked by the only person on board he could tell the person was a blind man. Because the man was wearing sunglasses and a seeing eye dog was lying quietly underneath the seat in front of him. The blind man had flown this flight frequently because the pilot could call him by name. The pilot asked, “Keith, we’re in Sacramento for almost an hour. Would you like to get off and stretch your legs? The blind man said no but he asked the pilot if he could take his dog for a walk.
What the pilot did not know was, all the people in the gate area came to a complete standstill when they saw him, because the pilot got off the plane with a seeing eye dog and a pair of sunglasses on. It caused a panic between passengers that they thought the pilot was a blind man. They not only tried to change planes, but also wanted to change airlines! It took time for the pilot and flight attendants to explain to passengers and calm them down. Later the aircraft took off again.

corrections.before: two generators failed leaving no lateral navigation On February 8, 2025, a One Air Boeing 7 47 400 freighter, performing flight 2 1 1 from London Heathrow (UK) to Hong Kong (China), was climbing out of Heathrow's Runway 09R when the crew stopped the climb at FL2 5 0, already over the North Sea reporting they had lost two of their four generators and requested radar vectors advising they had no lateral navigation left. On May 29th 2024 the AAIB reported the aircraft experienced failures on two electrical busses and lost all pitot heating. The aircraft diverted to Amsterdam due to marginal weather conditions at Heathrow. The occurrence has been rated a serious incident. On Feb 10th 2025 the AAIB reported in an interim statement: "The aircraft departed in weather of rain, thick cloud, and icing conditions. The crew began descending the aircraft from FL2 5 0 and experienced unreliable flight instrument indications. They diverted the aircraft to Amsterdam Schipol Airport, which had clear weather." The investigation is still ongoing.

corrections.before:
Lately I was on a VFR flight. we were passing within Aerodrome Traffic Zone under the control of Local Approach, visibility was good, and there was not too much traffic on the frequency.
The controller requested a position report by asking if we were over an Island, the feature cannot be found on the half million chart and I was not familiar with it. So I looked for it and asked for clarification. During the period a potential Airprox developed. Fortunately the pilot noted it and avoided it by an evasive maneuver.
The pilot and I were both annoyed by the controller for using an unrecognizable local feature which caused confusion and distraction for us. We were squawking 7000 Mode C, so our position should be known. If not, or if there were too much traffic on screen, the controller should have asked for a specific squawk.
Controllers should know that non-local pilots only navigate according to charted features. To avoid accidents, local knowledge should be taken seriously.

corrections.before:
A visual approach is an ATC authorization for aircraft on IFR flight plan to proceed visually to the airport, even to the landing. It is not an instrument approach procedure, and there is no missed approach segment. Even when an aircraft is being vectored for an instrument approach, controllers may initiate or pilots may request a visual approach if the pilot reports the airport or runway in sight. 
Before clearing an aircraft for a visual approach, controllers should ensure that weather conditions at the airport are VFR, and they need to resolve potential conflicts with all other aircraft. The pilot must have either the airport or the preceding aircraft in sight. This approach must be authorized and under ATC facility.

On impact with the ground, the nose gear collapsed, and the right main gear separated from the aircraft, puncturing the fuel tank and penetrating the cabin, causing a major fuel leak and the release of oxygen gas.
